object.description: The first page of the paper in which a twenty-six-year-old patent clerk in Bern replaced Newton's absolute space and time. Einstein starts from an everyday puzzle: moving a magnet past a coil or the coil past the magnet gives the same current, yet the physics of the day described the two cases differently. From that he takes two assumptions, that the laws of physics are the same for every observer moving at constant speed and that light travels at the same speed for all of them, and works out the consequences in thirty pages: moving clocks run slow, moving rods shrink, events simultaneous for one observer are not for another, and nothing with mass reaches the speed of light. The paper cites no earlier work and thanks only his friend Michele Besso. It reached the Annalen der Physik on 30 June 1905 and appeared on 26 September; a three-page sequel in November added the equation later written as E = mc². The theory became known as special relativity when Einstein generalised it to gravity in 1915.
facts: One of four papers Einstein published in 1905, his 'miracle year', alongside the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion and E = mc².
Written outside any university: Einstein was a 'technical expert, third class' at the Swiss patent office.
The word 'relativity' appears only as the 'principle of relativity'; Einstein did not name the theory.
The equations rediscovered Lorentz's transformations but gave them a wholly new meaning: there is no ether and no absolute rest.
